t: on their own. Separately from the Torah scroll.
and they cover them with leather. They enclose the passages in boxes made of leather, called batim (for how they are made see below 3:2-4).
the tip of a letter. A small part of the letter, such as its upper edge.
it invalidates all of them. If it is missing, all four passages are invalid.
and eight in their covering and the tying of their straps. These are explained below 3:1.
that they be written with ink. Below, halachot 4-5.
and that they be written on parchment. Below, halachot 6-11.
the making of the ink. How it is made.
they gather the smoke of oils. They collect the soot produced by burning oils (see Responsa of the Rambam 136).
and knead. To work into a paste.
and soak. They soak in water.
and pound. They crush.
thin pieces. Thin lumps.
he soaks it in gall-nut water. He dissolves the pieces of ink in water in which gall nuts (growths of the oak or terebinth tree) were soaked.
for if you wipe it, it will be erased. Ink made in this way can be erased (wiped off with water) without leaving a mark.
all three of them. A Torah scroll, tefillin and a mezuzah.
and kalkantos. Copper oxide, which fixes the ink so that it is not easily erased.
if so. That after the fact one may use also kalkantos and gall-nut water.
dyes. Coloring substances.
three hides. From an animal's hide one can produce three kinds of surfaces used for writing, as he explains.
and remove the hair. They remove the animal's hair.
that they gather the hide. They shrink and harden it.
and they split it along its thickness into two. They peeled it into two layers.
the tanners. Those who process hides.
the side facing the hair. The part of the hide adjacent to the hair.
the side facing the flesh. The inner side of the hide.
on the place of the hair. On the outer side, where the hair was.
on the place of the flesh. On the side facing the animal's flesh.
as a mitzvah. In the first instance.
the foulness. The dirt and stench.
whose foulness does not cease through tanning. Where the tanning process does not suffice to remove its filth.
for their sake. With the intention of fulfilling the mitzvah.
on his own understanding. He has independent intention that does not depend on what he was told.
anything that requires an act for its own sake. For example, spinning the strands of tzitzit (Hilchot Tzitzit 1:11) and writing a get (Hilchot Gerushin 3:15-16).
and a mezuzah does not require tanning for its sake. This law was not stated regarding it (for the reason see Responsa of the Rambam 334).
with ruling. Before writing, one scores the lines on the parchment with a knife so that the writing will be straight.
because they are covered. Enclosed in the tefillin casing.
not from writing. From memory.
for everyone recites them. These passages are known by heart.
a min. One who denies the existence of the Creator and His unity (as detailed in Hilchot Teshuvah 3:7).

they shall be burned. They have no sanctity, because the min does not believe in the sanctity of the Name and writes the names of God like other words, so the Name was not sanctified. And it is a mitzvah to destroy them so as to leave no trace of the minim and their deeds (Hilchot Yesodei HaTorah 6:8).
an apostate. One who abandoned his religion (see Hilchot Teshuvah 3:9).
an informer. One who denounces his fellow to the gentiles (see ibid. 3:12).
anyone who is commanded about the tying and believes in it may write. Women, slaves, minors and gentiles are not commanded about tying tefillin, and an apostate and an informer do not believe in it.
found in the hand of a min... they are to be hidden away. Because it is doubtful whether the min wrote them or someone else.
found in the hand of a gentile, they are valid. For a gentile ordinarily does not write tefillin, and presumably an Israelite wrote them.
for more than their value. At a price higher than their worth (similar to redeeming captives, see Hilchot Matnot Aniyim 8:12).
azkarah. One of the holy Names (for the list see Hilchot Yesodei HaTorah 6:2).
he may not interrupt. That he not turn his mind from the intention (compare Hilchot Kriat Shema 2:16).
two or three Names. He wrote several names of God one after another.
one who dips the quill. The writing instrument, which he dips in ink.
he should not begin with that Name. For at the start of using ink it may drip from the quill and spoil the writing.
he writes it between the lines. He writes it between the lines of the text.
the place of a scraping. A place where there was a word and it was scraped off.
the place of an erasure. A place where the ink was erased with water.
to turn the sheet face down. To place the written side downward, which is a way of disgrace.
folds it. He folds it so that the writing is covered.
is believed to forfeit all his payment. And the buyer is not obligated to pay him for his work on the basis of his words.
to cause a loss to the buyer. To cause the buyer a loss in order to vex him.
and he imagined etc.. He mistakenly supposed that he would receive all his payment except for the payment for writing the Names.
he has no payment at all. In such a situation, where the hide is not valid, it is clear that he will receive no payment at all, and if he says so we assume he is telling the truth.
in Assyrian script. The Hebrew script of today.
in the books. In Torah scrolls.
even in Greek. Also in Greek script and language.
and Greek has already vanished from the world. The Greek language of which the Sages spoke no longer exists.
for the hide does not surround it on its four sides. For there is no blank margin on all its sides.
not a wise man. Who guesses the text on his own.
and not a fool. Who, because of a slight change, no longer understands.
dalet. The letter dalet.
so that the reader may run through them. So that he can read quickly and easily.
for the ink passes over it. The ink covers the hole.
bird skin. Although it has holes, they are small and are covered by the ink.
a hole in the leg of a letter so that it was severed. The hole cut through the leg of the letter and shortened it.
the size of a small letter. The remaining letter can be read as a complete, small letter.
in four compartments joined in a single hide. In four cells made from one piece of leather (for the method of making see below 3:2-3).
in four columns. Four columns on the same parchment.
the closed (setumah) passage. A passage that begins in the middle of a line.
the open (petuchah) passage. A passage that begins on a new line (for the details of the laws of these passages see below 8:1-2).
with full and defective spelling. One may not change the full or defective spelling of the words.
the checked one. That has no errors.
and it cannot be corrected. For in tefillin one cannot add letters after writing (above 1:16; for the law of a Torah scroll see below 7:13).
like zayins standing on the letter. The crowns look like the shape of a thin zayin standing upright on top of the letter (below 7:8).
a closed mem. A final mem, closed on all sides.
an expert. One skilled in making tefillin.
cells. The tefillin boxes within which the passages are placed.
this man is presumed. This man is presumed to be a seller of valid tefillin.
bundles upon bundles. Different bundles of pairs of tefillin (see Commentary on the Mishnah, Eruvin 10:1).
he need not check them again. For checking a mezuzah see below 5:9.
these belonged to my mother's father. These tefillin belonged to my mother's father.
that they be square. Having four sides.
their stitching is square. The stitching that closes the tefillin boxes should be straight and even on every side.
and its diagonal is square. The square must be exact, so that its diagonals are equal in length.
with a patch. A piece of cloth.
a passage for the strap from the leather of the covering. A place for the strap to pass through, made from the leather that covers the passages.
the tover. A folded edge.
its length like its width like its height. A cube, equal on all its faces.

and they insert the leather between each and every groove. In this way four separate cells (compartments) are formed in the leather. And they use a long piece of leather, so that there remains leather free also for closing the tefillin, as explained in the next halachah.
and they crease it etc.. They crease the leather at the sides into the shape of the letter shin.
and the form of a shin that has four heads. This is an ancient tradition (Shimusha Rabbah), and various explanations have been given for it.
the mold. The form, the template.
and the leather is found to have four empty cells. The grooves in the wood form four hollows within the leather.
and they turn back some of the leather from below. They fold the leather that remains over the hollows.
and they leave from the leather below a place where the strap enters. From this leather they leave something like a loop through which the tefillin strap passes.
the arrangement of the passages. The order of placing the four passages in the tefillin.
the last passage. According to their order in the Torah.
the reader whose face is opposite the face of the one wearing. The person standing facing the one wearing the tefillin, who reads the passages in the tefillin.
reads in order. According to the order of their writing in the Torah.

like this. The diagram here shows the order of the passages from the wearer's side. The place of the strap marked in the diagram is the ma'aboret (strap passage), and its marking is meant to show that the tefillin are displayed as viewed from behind.
columns. Columns.
like a Torah scroll. Like a Torah scroll, which is written in columns.
in their order in the Torah. According to the order in which they are written in the Torah.
when he rolls up the passages. In order to insert them into the cells.
line. A line.
even from their carcasses and torn animals. And they need not be slaughtered properly.
and the sheets of a Torah scroll. As explained below 9:13.
three stitches. Three seams.
their thread goes around from both sides. The seam is doubled so that the sinew encircles the base of the box above and below.
the groove of the head tefillin. The groove separating one cell from the next.
up to the place of the stitching. The place where the tefillin are sewn, that is, the base of the box.
so that four heads are visible to all. So that it is evident there are four separate cells.
on the leather. At the bottom of the groove.
a thread. A thin string.
and it is a widespread custom. Common.
to pass a sinew from the stitching sinews etc.. They use the sinew with which they sewed the box and pass it between the three grooves.
the length of a barley grain. The length of a barley kernel (about half a thumb's width, below 9:9).
from here and from here. On both sides of the neck.
in its tover. The fold of leather at the edge of the box.
and he encircles the measure of his head. He measures from the strap so that it will encircle his head, and then ties.
in the form of a dalet. In the shape of the letter dalet.
it goes up and down within the knot. The strap is loose within the knot so that he can adjust it to his arm and tighten it.
and they are on the inside. Turned toward his body and not visible.
and it is a disgrace for him. For it looks like blood, and perhaps it is unclean blood.
like the box. The same color the box (the tefillin casing) is dyed. [Note: The word noy is written and vocalized by the Rambam in his Commentary on the Mishnah as no'i.]
matzah. Hide that was not tanned at all.

for their making is like their writing etc.. The making of tefillin is considered writing, because it includes making the letter shin, and therefore it is valid only by an Israelite, as with writing (above 1:13).
as we said. Above, halachah 2.
for anyone unfit to write them. Those who are unfit are explained above 1:13.

for one does not descend from a greater sanctity to a lesser sanctity. And the head tefillin has greater sanctity than the hand tefillin (perhaps because through it "the Name of God is called upon you" is fulfilled). For this rule see also below 5:1; Hilchot Tefillah 11:14; Hilchot Tzitzit 1:7.
to return it to a hand tefillin. To change it to a hand tefillin.
he patches it with leather until it becomes one. He covers the four cells with leather so that they look like one box.
whose stitches were torn. The seams closing the box ripped.
one beside the other. On both sides of the box (since the stitching is doubled and holds the box above and below, as explained above, halachah 10).
old ones. That may tear easily.

as long as the face of the tablet remains, they are valid. "Face of the tablet" is the term for the leather of the base of the cells, which is like a square board. As long as it remains attached to the cells, the tefillin are valid.
anything by which one can hold some of the leather... and hang the tefillin from it. They hold the tefillin by the torn part and check whether it is strong enough not to tear from the tefillin.
and the remnants of the strap. What remains of the strap after it tore.
until its length and width are the required measure. See above, halachah 12.
the face of the leather of the straps. Its outer side, dyed black.
the hair opposite the face. The hair above the forehead.
where a baby's brain pulses. Where an infant's skull is soft.
at the height of the nape. At the upper end of the nape, where it meets the skull.
the swelling flesh. The muscle.
when he presses his elbow to his ribs. When he brings his arm against his body.
tefillah. The hand tefillin.
on the palm of his hand. On the palm of the hand.
the way of heresy. This is how those who deny the Oral Torah put on tefillin.
left-handed. A lefty.
from oral tradition. Oral tradition.
the head tefillin does not hold up the hand tefillin etc.. And he may put on each of them separately, without needing the other.
if he put on both, he recites one blessing. Although they are two mitzvot, their subject is one (Responsa of the Rambam 288).
to converse. To speak.
he must recite a second blessing. The first blessing does not count for him, because he interrupted with speech.
as long as he puts them on. Every time he puts them on.

he recites the blessing over them before making them. One recites the blessing over the performance of a mitzvah close to the time of its performance (for this principle see Hilchot Berachot 11:2-3 ff.).
after placing it on the biceps. In order to bring the blessing as close as possible to the act.
for their tying is their making. The tying is the act of the mitzvah.
in the case. In the pouch in which they are kept.
he should not place etc.. He should not place them one on top of the other with the hand tefillin underneath.
he may encounter. Come upon.
that he leaves it. He leaves it in order to put on the hand tefillin first.
that he prepared to put tefillin in. He designated it for keeping the tefillin.
and it is forbidden to hang the tefillin. On a hook or pole and the like, which is not a respectful way.
from days to days. The language of the verse: "You shall keep this statute at its appointed time from year to year," and the verse is expounded as referring to the mitzvah of tefillin.
and they shall be a sign for you. Tefillin serve as a sign between Israel and God.
and Sabbaths and festivals are themselves a sign. The very sanctity of the day is considered a sign, and there is no need for tefillin.
from the time he can see his fellow... and recognize him. When there is enough daylight for this.
he transgresses a prohibition, as it says: "and you shall keep". This language of command to be careful is considered a negative prohibition (Sefer HaMitzvot, Shoresh 8).
he places his hand over them. He covers them so that the public will not see him.
until he reaches his house and removes them. They did not trouble him to remove them on the way, since by the basic law he may remain in his tefillin (as explained in the previous halachah).
in the study hall. Which is located outside the city.

and the day became sanctified upon him. The Sabbath entered, which is not a time for tefillin (above halachah 10), and he does not want to leave the tefillin in the study hall, where they are not guarded; nor can he remove them in the study hall and carry them to his home because of the Sabbath.
and if there is a house near the wall... he places them there. He does not wait until he reaches his house, for as soon as he can remove them in a guarded place, he must do so.
and they were found on him in order to guard them, it is permitted. Not to remove them even in the first instance, as explained regarding one sitting in the study hall.
anyone exempt from reciting the Shema. Those exempt are explained in Hilchot Kriat Shema 4:1-3.
those with intestinal illness etc.. For while wearing tefillin one must keep the body clean (below halachah 15).
priests during the service. The Temple service (and if they wish, they may wear the head tefillin, see Hilchot Kelei HaMikdash 10:6).
and Levites when they sing the song on the platform. A place in the Temple on which the Levites sang during the offering of the sacrifice (Hilchot Beit HaBechirah 6:6).
during their ma'amad in the Temple. The Israelite representatives present in the Temple during the offering of the sacrifices (Hilchot Kelei HaMikdash 6:1).
are exempt from prayer and from tefillin. Because of their occupation with the Temple service.
to touch his tefillin. To touch them from time to time, to remember them (for the implications for the laws of Shabbat see Hilchot Shabbat 19:26).
for the plate has only one Name. On the plate (tzitz) worn by the high priest was written "Holy to the Lord" (Exodus 28:36).
and these have. In the passages in the tefillin the Name of God appears twenty-one times.
wrapped in his hand. He holds them and does not put them on.
he removes them and places them on his table. For it is not respectful to dine while wearing tefillin.
until he washes his hands. At the end of the meal, for the final water (see Hilchot Berachot 6:1-2).
in the holes. In the cracks in the wall next to the lavatory.
at a distance. From the lavatory.
and rolls them in his garment like a Torah scroll. He wraps the tefillin in his garment as one rolls up a Torah scroll.
the fixed one. Designated for this.
where no splashes bounce onto him. Drops of urine do not splash back onto him.
rolled up. As explained in the previous halachah.
and urine does not finish. Leaving the body.
except while sitting. For then a person is not worried about soiling himself and finishes his needs.
loose earth. Soft soil from which drops do not splash, and a person is not worried about getting dirty.
he should stand on a slope. He should urinate in the downhill direction.
and not enough of the day remains to put them on after he leaves. There is not enough time left in the day to put on the tefillin after he comes out of the lavatory.
he should not enter with rolled-up tefillin in his garment. For in any case he would not use them again afterward.
and he places them in their case if it has a handbreadth. In the hollow of the case, so that the tefillin are in a separate domain.

in a vessel that is not their case, even if it has no handbreadth. For a vessel not intended for keeping the tefillin is separate from them, and therefore it separates between them and the outside (see below halachah 24).
the first wall. Of excrement or urine.
on the box. The body of the tefillin box.
until he washes his hands and removes them. Only after washing his hands does he take off the tefillin.
because hands are busy. And presumably they touched dirty places.

a person should not walk in a cemetery with tefillin on his head. Because of the sanctity of tefillin (see Hilchot Kriat Shema 3:2. The same law applies to entering with a Torah scroll, below 10:6; Hilchot Avel 14:13).
even within four cubits. Even though he is not in the cemetery itself.
until he is four cubits away. While he is still far, before he comes within four cubits.
until he removes the load. For when a person carries a load on his head, it is a disgrace to the tefillin.
even a kerchief. Which is a light load.
even if his wife is with him in bed. In such a case there is no prohibition against marital relations.
a house in which there are tefillin or a Torah scroll. See also below 10:7.
house. Room.

if the second vessel was also designated for them... they are considered as one vessel. If the second vessel too is designated for keeping the tefillin, it is not a sufficient covering, since everything is considered a single covering.
Rav, the disciple of our holy Rabbi. The Babylonian amora Rav (Rabbi Abba), who studied Torah with Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi, called "our holy Rabbi" (and see Hilchot De'ot 2:4).
as if he gives false testimony against himself. For he reads the passages that command tefillin, but in practice does not fulfill them.
transgresses eight positive commandments. He nullifies eight positive commandments.
"the Lord is upon them, they shall live". And it is expounded: when the Name of God is placed upon them (in tefillin), they will merit life.
on one page. In one column.
a space... about half a fingernail. A space between the writing and the edge of the sheet, about half a fingernail's width.
like a tail. Lines long at the top and short at the bottom.
like a circle. The lines form the shape of a circle.
like a dome. Like a tent, with lines long at the bottom and short at the top.
he put one passage before another. He wrote the second passage and beneath it the first.
from the margin of a scroll. Blank parchment left at the edge of a Torah scroll (see Hilchot Shabbat 23:27 and Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTum'ot 9:6 for further laws regarding the margin of a scroll).
for one does not descend from a greater sanctity to a lesser sanctity. For this rule see above 3:17; Hilchot Tefillah 11:14; Hilchot Tzitzit 1:7.

and it is a mitzvah to make the space... a closed passage. As the passage "And it shall be, if you listen" is written in the Torah (see the list of open and closed passages below 8:4; for the form of open and closed passages see there, halachot 1-2).

valid, since it is not adjacent to it in the Torah. Unlike tefillin (above 2:2), where the passages "Sanctify" and "And it shall be when He brings you" are adjacent to each other, and therefore the form of the passages is indispensable (Ma'aseh Rokeach).
the crowns. The crowns of the letters, as explained above 2:8.
without ruling. Without marking the lines, as explained above 1:12.
that he was not careful with full and defective spelling. He was not careful about the exact spelling of the words (see above 1:16 and below 7:11 regarding tefillin and a Torah scroll).
that he added on the inside. But on the outside it is customary to add, as explained in the next halachah.
or seals. Various shapes used for amulets.
they perform a great mitzvah... for the benefit of themselves. Compare Hilchot Avodah Zarah 11:12.
on the earth. The words at the end of the second passage.
in a line. A line.
to write it. The mezuzah.
when they fold it. They fold the mezuzah to put it into the mezuzah case.
from the end of the line to its beginning. Similar to tefillin (above 3:7).
the doorpost of the entrance. The vertical post of the doorway.
for its affixing is the mitzvah. One recites the blessing at the time of performing the mitzvah itself and not at the time of the preparations for it (see Hilchot Berachot 11:8).
he hung it on a stick. He attached it to a stick next to the doorpost, but it is not attached to the doorpost itself.
behind the door. On the wall behind the door, and not on the doorpost.
and he inserted the mezuzah like a bolt. He laid the mezuzah horizontally, like a locking bar.

he hollowed it out a handbreadth, it is invalid. He carved into the doorpost to a depth of a handbreadth; at this depth it is not considered placed "on the doorposts of your house" but inside the post.
and he set up everything. He prepared a doorway from these reeds, in which a mezuzah was already placed.

that the affixing of the mezuzah preceded the making of the doorpost. The mezuzah was affixed when the doorway did not yet exist, and at the time of its affixing the mitzvah was not fulfilled (see Hilchot Tzitzit 1:12-13).
in the shevu'a. In seven years.
in the Jubilee. In fifty years, because the public was not burdened to check as much as the individual.
thirty days. Only after that is he considered as dwelling in the house.

One who rents a house in the Land of Israel is obligated in mezuzah immediately. Because of the settlement of the Land of Israel; therefore as soon as he rents, he is considered as dwelling in the house.
the renter must bring a mezuzah. See also Hilchot Sechirut 6:3.
even if he would be paying money for affixing it. Even if it will cost him money.
he should not take it in his hand and leave. For it is not proper to neglect the mitzvah with one's own hands.
ten conditions etc.. Their details will be explained in this chapter.
that it have four cubits by four cubits. The size of the house must be at least four by four cubits.
two doorposts. A doorway with two posts at its sides.
lintel. A beam above the doorway, resting on the doorposts.
a secular house. One not designated for sacred purposes.

and if it has enough to square four by four cubits etc.. If it has sufficient area, so that were it built as a square it would be sixteen square cubits. Or it means that within the perimeter of the house a square of four cubits by four cubits can fit.
its length exceeds its width. Built as a rectangle.
that has three walls and a roof. And the fourth side is open.
side posts. Pillars.
and they were not made for the sake of doorposts. They do not constitute the doorway of the portico.
if the height of the doorposts is ten handbreadths or more, it is obligated. For the house has two doorposts of the required height, and the arch is considered the lintel.
and if they are not ten. Even though together with the arch there is a height of ten handbreadths.

because it has no lintel. This doorway would be obligated in mezuzah only if its height is calculated as including the height of the arch, in which case the arch is part of the doorposts and is not considered a lintel.

It seems to me that if the roofing was opposite the doorway, it is obligated in a mezuzah. For if the roofing is above the doorway, then there is a doorway here that is obligated in mezuzah, even though the rest of the house is not roofed.
opposite the doorway. Above the doorway.
and the doors are set up. For without a door there is no obligation of mezuzah (as noted above, halacha 1), so the doors must be set up first (Responsa of the Rambam 35; and see above 5:8).
the Temple Mount. Which is surrounded by a wall (Hilchot Beit HaBechirah 5:1).
the chambers. Various rooms in the Temple.
and the courtyards. The various precincts of the Temple, such as the Women's Courtyard and the Israelites' Courtyard.
which have no residential quarters. They have no area designated for people to live in.
a village synagogue where guests sleep. It has a place designated for lodging guests.

except for the Nicanor Gate and what is inside it. The eastern entrance gate to the Israelites' Courtyard in the Temple, and the inner doorways from it leading to the Palhedrin chamber (whose identity is not clear to us). They are obligated in mezuzah because through them one enters a house that is obligated in mezuzah (below, halachot 7-8).
a dwelling for the High Priest during the seven days of separation. During the seven days before Yom Kippur, when he did not live in his house with his wife (Hilchot Avodat Yom HaKippurim 1:3).
storehouse. A warehouse.
that is designated for you. That a person designates for his personal use.
it has designation for human dwelling. The cattle shed is also designated for human use.
gatehouse. A booth next to the gate of the house, where the doorkeeper sits.
portico. Even if it has doorposts (see above, halacha 3).

and if houses that are obligated in mezuzah open into these places etc.. If these places lead into the obligated house, their doorways are considered doorways of the house that is obligated in mezuzah, and they too are obligated in mezuzah.
courtyard gates. The gate of a courtyard into which several houses open.
alley gates. The gate of the street into which several courtyards open, with houses inside them.
a gate that opens from the garden into the courtyard is obligated. Because the courtyard is obligated due to the houses that open into it, as mentioned at the beginning of the halacha.
and the immersion house. A mikveh.
and the tannery. A place for processing hides, which is foul-smelling.
because they are not made for respectable dwelling. Rather, they are used in a degrading manner.
the festival sukkah on the festival. In which one sits on the festival of Sukkot.
two potters' sukkot, one inside the other. Potters would make two sukkot: the inner one fixed for their dwelling, and the outer one temporary, for work and for selling the pottery.
house. The lower floor.
and upper room. The upper floor.
is obligated in a mezuzah. Although a study hall or a synagogue is exempt from mezuzah (above, halacha 6), here it is obligated because it is also a doorway to his house.

a doorway between two houses. Where it is not known which is the inner and which the outer (for example, where both have another doorway to the public domain). Since the mezuzah is to be placed on the right of one entering (below, halacha 12), one must decide which house to follow.
the place where the hinge is visible with it. The house within which is the hinge that connects the door to the wall is the inner one, and by it the mezuzah is fixed on the right of one entering.
the space of the doorway, in the handbreadth next to the outside. When the doorway is several handbreadths thick, the mezuzah is fixed in its space, close to the edge facing outward.
he will encounter. He will meet, run into.
and awaken from his sleep etc.. The Rambam similarly describes the shofar (Hilchot Teshuvah 3:4).
and his error. His preoccupation and absorption.

And now write for yourselves this song, meaning etc.. This verse was said about the song of Ha'azinu, but since the Torah is not written in separate sections (below, halacha 14), it must be interpreted as a commandment to write the entire Torah, including this song.
as if he received it from Sinai. For writing the Torah with his own hand is like a renewed receiving of the Torah.
the one who corrects. Who emends, so that it is written correctly.
in addition to the book he had when he was a commoner. In addition to the book he is commanded to write as an ordinary person (see also Hilchot Melachim 3:1).
and they correct it from the Torah scroll of the Temple Courtyard. They verify that it is written correctly, according to the Torah scroll that was in the Temple.
he places it in his treasure house. In the treasury, which need not be in use.
after he becomes king he must write two Torah scrolls. For the scroll that is with the king is always called in the Torah "a copy of the Torah" (Deuteronomy 17:18), that is, a second copy.
it shall not leave him except at night etc.. In places and times that are not fit for reading (see also Hilchot Melachim 3:1).
without ruling lines. Without scoring the lines on the parchment with a knife to straighten the writing (above 1:12).
part of it on gevil and part on klaf. He wrote the scroll on different types of hides (see above 1:6-7).
fine, proper writing is most beautiful. For the sake of embellishing the mitzvah.
he should leave between each word the space of a small letter. Between words he leaves a space the size of a small letter.
and between each line the space of a line. Between lines he leaves a space the height of a line.
and this is the width of each page. That the width of the page (column) is the length of the line.
that the page not be like a letter. Like a letter, whose lines are short.
so that his eyes will not wander over the writing. For if the lines are too long, it is hard to find the beginning of the next line.

he should not make the writing smaller because of the space between one section and another. He should not shrink the letters in order to leave room for the spaces required between sections (see below 8:1-2), for that is not an embellishment of the scroll.
it happens to him. When he reaches the end of the line.
he should not write two inside the page and three outside the page. Two letters within the boundary of the column and three extending outward beyond it, for this is not attractive.
and he begins from the beginning of the line. He writes the word at the beginning of the next line.
he should not throw it between the pages. It is forbidden to write it between the columns.
four lines empty without writing. A gap of four blank lines.
in the middle of a line at the end of the page. In the middle of the last line of the column.

and if many lines remain on the page, he shortens and ascends etc.. If he sees that he will not reach the bottom of the page, he writes short lines, beginning to write at the start of the line but not finishing it, and arranges the writing so as to end the Torah at the end of the page in the middle of a line.
the large letters etc.. Variations in the writing of letters as transmitted in the scribal tradition.
the dots. Those that have dots above them.
the bent pe's. Those that have an extra curl inward.
the crowns. Kinds of crowns marked on top of the letters.
and all the crowns are in the shape of a zayin. A thin line with a thickened head (see also above 2:8).
but as a preferred mitzvah. All of these are for the embellishment and beauty of the Torah scroll.
as long as he did not join one letter to another. As long as he did not make letters stick together.
and did not omit and did not add. Of the letters.
he spoiled. He corrupted.
and did not change the open and closed sections. In the manner of writing the sections (below chapter 8).
and the scribes practiced them and it is a tradition in their hands etc.. This is how they were accustomed to write Torah scrolls, and this tradition was passed from generation to generation.
the number of lines. The number of rows.
at the beginnings of the lines above the Song of the Sea etc.. In the passage before the Song of the Sea, at the top of the column, the lines should begin with these words.
wrote the full as defective or the defective as full. He omitted or added the vowel letters (aleph, heh, vav, yod).
a word that is read one way and written another, and he wrote it as it is read. A word that must be read differently from how it is written, and he wrote it according to the reading tradition.

an open or closed section etc.. That one distinguishes between paragraphs (sections) that begin at the start of a line and those that begin in the middle of a line (explained below 8:1-2), and if he changed them, it is invalid.
who wrote the song like the rest of the writing. He wrote the Song of the Sea and the Song of Ha'azinu not in their special form (see below, end of chapter 8).
but like a chumash of the chumashim with which children are taught. It is indeed a holy book, but it does not have the sanctity of a Torah scroll, and it is not read from in public (below 10:1).
that is not corrected. That has an error that invalidates it.
or he should store it away. By burial in the ground (see below 10:3).
four he must store away. And he should not correct it, because it is not attractive for a scroll to have many corrections.
most of the scroll is corrected. Most of the pages of the scroll were written properly without any error.

and even one page remains from that corrupted remainder without four mistakes. That part of the scroll is entirely corrupted with four errors per page, but on one page of it there are fewer than that (see Yad Peshutah).

for he turns out to be hanging the letters that he forgot between the lines. If he omitted a letter, he may write it above the place where it is missing, between the lines (above 1:16). Many corrections of this kind are not attractive for a scroll and make reading difficult.
because he scrapes and does not hang. He scrapes the ink off the parchment, and such corrections are not noticeable as hanging letters are.
each chumash. In separate scrolls of the individual chumashim.
and they do not have the sanctity of a complete Torah scroll. They are not as holy as the complete scroll, and one does not read from them in public (below 10:1).
a scroll by itself that contains sections. That does not contain a whole chumash.
a scroll for a child to learn from. That a child will learn from.
and if he intends to complete a chumash with it. If he intends to complete the scroll into a full chumash.
a scroll with three words to a line. He wrote every three words on a separate line.
it is permitted to join Torah, Prophets and Writings in one volume. So that they are connected in one long scroll.

for if he wants to cut, he may cut. He is permitted to join the books together, even though this involves lowering the sanctity of the Torah (below, halacha 16), because he may also separate the books later if he wishes.
and the order of the Prophets etc.. This is the order of the books of the Prophets according to the tradition of the Sages (which is not chronological, but by subject).
Lamentations. Eichah.
the Scroll. Esther.
with ruling lines. Scoring the lines on the parchment, to straighten the writing (above, halacha 4).
even if he wrote them on paper. Although it is not a valid scroll, he must rule lines out of respect for the holy writings.
and it is permitted to write three words without ruling lines. For writing only three words is not considered writing holy texts (see above, halacha 14; and compare Hilchot Yibbum VeChalitzah 4:35).
its sanctity is not like the sanctity of a Torah scroll. And one does not read from it in public.

the law of an addition is like the law of an omission. Just as omitting from a complete scroll invalidates it, so that it does not have the status of a Torah scroll, so too adding to it invalidates it (compare Hilchot Shechitah 8:11).
an open section. That has an "open" gap between it and the section before it.
if he finished in the middle of the line. If he finished the previous section in the middle of a line.
from the beginning of the second line. From the start of the next line.
like this. In manuscripts these examples are drawn as lines without words. In the illustrations here the examples are shown with words, as in the edition of Rabbi Yosef Kafih.
so that there remains of the line a space of nine letters. That there remained in the line he wrote in a space of more than nine letters, which is the minimum gap between sections (above 7:10).
he leaves the second line entirely blank without writing. He leaves the next line completely empty, and begins the open section from the beginning of the line after it.
and a closed section. Where the gap between it and the section before it is "closed."
he leaves a space of the measure. That is, nine letters.

and he begins to write at the end of the line from the beginning of the section, which is closed. The first word of the closed section he writes at the end of the same line in which he finished the previous section.
he leaves all of it blank. And does not write further on that line.

and leaves a little space from the start of the second line. He need not leave the entire measure of the gap at the beginning of the line, since he already left it at the end of the previous line; a small space suffices.
and he begins to write the closed section from the middle of a line. That is, he does not begin at the start of the line.
he leaves from the beginning of the second line the measure of the space. For he did not leave it in the previous line.
as we have explained. Above 7:12-13.
or changed the forms of the songs. That he did not write them in their special form but as usual.
to remove the entire page in which he erred. And to write another in its place, correctly.
and likewise the masters of the Masorah. Who collected the fine points of the versions of the Torah, including the open and closed sections.
are divided... like the disagreement of the books on which they rely. Each one relies on a different book.
in order to correct all the books according to them and to emend from them. So that it will be possible to correct Torah scrolls according to what will be explained below.
is the book known in Egypt. An accurate book that was well known in Egypt.
which contains the twenty-four books. All the books of Torah, Prophets and Writings.
because Ben Asher corrected it. Aaron ben Asher, one of the great masters of the Masorah, who lived in the tenth century CE.
as they copied it. According to the rules transmitted by the careful scribes up to his time (and perhaps it should be vocalized "that he copied it," that is, from the same source).
in a Torah scroll that I wrote according to halacha. About this scroll see further below 9:10-11.

in the form of a closed section. A space of at least nine letters (above, halacha 2). The first line as usual. A full line. And there is a space opposite writing and writing opposite the space. In relation to the line before it. To a child who is not accustomed. They test whether a child who is not familiar with the Scriptural verses manages to read it as one word, or whether it looks to him like two.
its length. The height of the sheet, which is the length of the scroll.
its circumference. The measure of the circumference of the sheets when they are rolled together.
and how much is its proper length. The fitting measure.
on gevil. Processed hide for writing (above 1:6).
and on klaf. A hide that has been split in its thickness, and it is the side opposite the flesh (above 1:7; and see there halachot 8-9).
or less or more etc.. For the measure of six handbreadths was stated only for gevil.
and reduced the writing. He made the letters smaller, to fit a smaller scroll.
and widened the writing. He made the letters larger, to fit a larger scroll.
the measure of the margin. The space left empty at the edges of the page, above, below and at the sides.
and between page and page. Between each column and the next.
and enough for sewing. The measure needed for sewing the sheets to one another, which does not serve as space between the sheets.
enough to roll a column. The measure needed for rolling the sheet once around the wooden poles at the beginning and end of the scroll, around which the scroll is rolled (and see below, halacha 14).
a person should plan. He should plan the format of the scroll in advance.
and he squares the hides equally. To make them sheets of uniform height.
the width of each hide. The height of the hide.
one measure for all. One measure for all the sheets.
he rolls the hides. He winds them together.
roll. A cylinder.
and he measures with a thread of wool dyed crimson. Which does not stretch, and so he measures the circumference of the roll accurately.
a straight ruler. A straight measuring rod.
until he knows how many fingerbreadths there are in each and every hide. That he know its exact length, in order to calculate the number of columns he will be able to write on it (below, halacha 6).
to test with them the measure of the writing. So that he will know what size of letters is suitable for that scroll.
and he writes on them one page. One column as a trial.
for the length of the page is seventeen fingerbreadths etc.. In a scroll whose height is six handbreadths, which is twenty-four fingerbreadths.
because he leaves a margin of three above and four below. As written above, halacha 2.

the width of the page is according to the writing. The width of the column is determined by the size of the letters, since it is determined by the length of a written line, which is thirty letters (above 7:4).
and likewise the number of lines on the page will come according to the writing. The number of lines in a column is also not fixed, but depends on the height of the letters (above 7:10).
he should measure the width of the page in the fingerbreadths of the ruler. He should measure the width of the column with the measuring rod.

and calculate how many pages will fit in the roll he rolled. He divides the total length of the roll by the width of a column with its margins, and thus knows how many columns of this size can be written.

and see how much was written on this page that he tested, out of the entire Torah. He checks the proportion between the amount he wrote and the rest of the Torah, according to the scroll he is copying from, and sees whether the expected number of columns will suffice.
and when three fingerbreadths of the hide remain etc.. If there remains at the edge of the sheet a blank space that cannot be made into another column, he cuts it off.

and let him not worry that in the end other hides will be added to him. He should not worry that he is reducing the scope of the scroll so that it will not match its height, since afterwards he will add other hides to complete the scroll, corresponding to those ends of the sheets that were counted in the length and cut off, and these will complete the circumference.

and he need not calculate this matter etc.. He need not calculate the amount of the ends he cut off in order to complete accordingly, because if he writes according to the writing calculated at the outset, the pages will complete the circumference properly.
and in the other measures of the entire Torah. Which is a basic measure for measures of length and volume (see Hilchot Tefillah 15:4).
the average. The medium.
one beside the other, crowded. Pressed close to each other.
with space. Not pressed close.
four fingerbreadths from this one. In the thumb, whose measure was explained.
and the Song of the Sea and the Song of Ha'azinu. For the columns in them must be wider, because of the form of the song (see above 9:6-7).

one thousand three hundred and sixty-six fingerbreadths. For each column six fingerbreadths are counted (above, halacha 6), and for two of them, those of the songs, two more fingerbreadths are added, so the calculation comes to one thousand three hundred and sixty (and for the additional six fingerbreadths see the next halacha).
for the margin at the beginning of the scroll and at its end. Which is rolled onto the wooden poles around which the scroll is wound (below, halacha 14).
and the hides on which we wrote are rams' hides. This is important because hides of another type, which have a different thickness, should not be compared with this calculation.
you will not need to toil. You will not need to bother to calculate anew.
but immediately its length will come to you as its circumference. Because the additions are negligible, and affect the circumference minimally.
fewer than three pages etc.. For shortening or lengthening the sheets is not an embellishment of the scroll.
he divides it. He cuts it, so that its length will be average.
but at the end of the scroll. One is not strict about this there, since at the end of a scroll there often are things that are not so attractive, caused by practical constraints.
with sinews of an animal... as tefillin are sewn. With threads made from sinews (see above 3:9).
even from their carcasses and treifot. For these too are of a pure species (above 1:10).
he does not sew the entire sheet from its beginning to its end. The sheets are not sewn to one another along their whole length.

so that the sheet not tear in its middle when he rolls. For if the sewing is complete, the sheet itself will tear if the scroll is overly stretched. But since gaps are left in the sewing, if the scroll is stretched the sewn spot will tear and it is easy to repair.
and he sews the hide he left at the beginning and at the end. At the two ends of the scroll (above, halacha 2, halacha 11).
and let him keep distance between the pole and the writing on the page. He should not wind all of the remaining margin around the pole.
within two lines he may sew. A tear entering from the edge of the parchment, from above or below, to a depth of two lines of the writing, he may sew and repair.

within three he may not sew... in an old one whose gall-nut treatment is not noticeable. The gall-nut is a growth formed on certain plants (oak, tamarisk and others) from which a substance is extracted that is used in processing parchment so that it will last a long time. When the gall treatment is not noticeable, it is a sign that the scroll is very worn, and a large sewing will not hold in it.
if the gevil is seen to be gall-treated, he may sew etc.. For it is a sign that the scroll is still in good condition, and the sewing will hold.
between page and page and between word and word he may sew. Even if the tear is deeper than two lines, for the tear does not affect the reading.
so that not one letter be missing or its form change. Because of the tear, since a missing letter invalidates the scroll (below 10:1).
like a chumash of the chumashim etc.. Which is a holy book, but not of the level of a complete Torah scroll (see above 7:14).

and even an old one, he may buy a new one with it. Although in this way he does not lower the proceeds of the scroll from their sanctity (see Hilchot Tefillah 11:14).
next to a Torah scholar. In the grave of a Torah scholar.
book wrappers. Which are wound around holy books, and have sanctity (see the next halacha).
shrouds. Garments in which the dead are dressed.
for a met mitzvah. A dead Jew who has no one to bury him, and whose burial needs fall on the public (compare Hilchot Avel 2:7).
case. The sheath in which the Torah scroll is placed.
and it was placed in it. For if it was prepared without being placed in it, it does not become sanctified (see also above 4:9).
and the ark or the tower. Different kinds of portable wooden cabinets in which a Torah scroll is placed (see Hilchot Tefillah 11:3 and the commentary there).
even though the scroll is inside the case. And it is not placed directly inside the ark or the tower.
the platforms. A raised structure in the center of the synagogue (Hilchot Tefillah there).
and the tablets. On which the form of the alphabet letters is written.
have no sanctity. Therefore there is no need to store them away if they wear out, and one may sell them and use the proceeds for secular purposes.
silver and gold pomegranates. Ornaments placed on the sheath of a Torah scroll.
to buy with their proceeds a Torah scroll or a chumash. Whose sanctity is greater (see Hilchot Tefillah 11:14).

the chumashim. The Torah written with each chumash separately (above 7:14). It does not have the sanctity of a Torah scroll and is unfit for public reading, and it is used for teaching children (above, halacha 1).
it is forbidden to throw them. From hand to hand or from place to place.
amulets. Parchment or paper on which verses or holy names are written as a charm (see Hilchot Shabbat 23:27).
unless they are covered with leather. For leather is considered a covering.
while he is naked. When a person is unclothed (see below, halacha 8 and the rulings and opinions there).
a person should not hold a Torah scroll in his arm and enter a bathhouse etc.. See also Hilchot Tefillin 4:23, Hilchot Keriat Shema 3:2.
house. Room.
in which there is a Torah scroll etc.. See also above 4:24.
that is not designated for it. That is not the vessel in which a Torah scroll is usually placed.
for words of Torah do not receive impurity. See also Hilchot Keriat Shema 4:8.
when he is walking. When someone is carrying the Torah scroll.
until the one who is walking with it stops when he reaches its place. Until the one carrying the Torah scroll stops when he places it in its place.
so that it be hidden from their eyes. So that they do not see it.
too much. A lot.
matters of the tablets of the covenant. Just as a special place was set aside for the tablets of the covenant and they were treated with honor and splendor, so one must treat every Torah scroll.
and he should not stretch out his legs. Sit with his legs toward the Torah scroll in a disrespectful way.
unless it was ten handbreadths higher than he. For when the scroll is ten handbreadths above his head, his back is not opposite the scroll and there is no disgrace in this.
